"You look for the assumption that makes a problem slow, or makes extra compute buy only more of the same. Ask which part
of the work waits on another part, and whether it must. Ask which quantity is measured, and whether a different but
related quantity would be cheaper to compute, easier to split, or more informative. Ask whether the unit of work is the
right one, or whether the work could be cut, merged or reordered. Ask whether the objective is the right one: the single
best answer, a ranking, a distribution, a rare tail, or a yes or no. Ask what is held fixed that need not be. Prefer
changes that alter what more compute buys over changes that only run the same work more times.

Here is a research problem as it was first written down, with the question it belongs to.
Root question: What limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could that be fixed with a shit ton of GPU parallelism?
Problem:
Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains.

Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost. Decide from the text above and what you know; do not use tools.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"reframes\"],\"properties\":{\"reframes\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"bottleneck\",\"assumption\",\"reframe\",\"question\",\"measure\",\"compute_after\",\"exact\",\"expected\",\"fails_if\",\"closest_prior\"],\"properties\":{\"bottleneck\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"assumption\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reframe\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"question\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"measure\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"compute_after\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"exact\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"expected\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"fails_if\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"closest_prior\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

The task: analyze a research problem about Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models requiring long MCMC chains, find where more compute doesn't help or only buys more of the same, propose up to three reframings with specific investigable questions, cheapest measurements, costs, etc.

Return only JSON matching the schema with fields: bottleneck, assumption, reframe, question, measure, compute_after, exact, expected, fails_if, closest_prior.

Let me think about the domain.

Rainfall-runoff models (e.g., GR4J, HBV, HYMOD, SAC-SMA) — calibrating parameters via MCMC (e.g., DREAM, Metropolis-Hastings). Long chains needed because: posterior is multimodal, parameters correlated, high-dimensional; also each likelihood evaluation requires running the model over a long time series (years of daily data), and MCMC is inherently sequential. GPU parallelism: could run many chains in parallel, but MCMC mixing time is the bottleneck — more chains of same length doesn't fix slow mixing; parallel chains only help if the bottleneck is number of samples, not autocorrelation time. Also the model itself is often fast (lumped models run in milliseconds) — so compute may not even be the blocker; the blocker is the geometry of the posterior (identifiability, equifinality) and the sequential nature of MCMC.

Key reframings:

1. Change the objective / what is measured: Instead of full posterior over parameters, ask for a yes/no or distribution of predictions (predictive distributions) — e.g., estimate posterior predictive quantities directly, or use rare-event estimation. Or reframe: instead of estimating the posterior, estimate the normalizing constant / evidence, or a tail quantity (prob of exceeding a flood threshold). Hmm.

2. Change unit of work: replace MCMC over the full time series with likelihood-free / surrogate approaches: train an emulator (neural net, GP) of the model via massive parallel GPU simulation (amortized — simulation is embarrassingly parallel), then run inference with neural posterior estimation (SBI — simulation-based inference, NPE). This converts sequential MCMC into embarrassingly parallel simulation, which is exactly what GPUs buy. Question: how many simulator runs does NPE need to reach the same posterior accuracy as a 10^5-step MCMC? Measure: simulate N runs in parallel, train NPE, compare posterior (e.g., C2ST or MMD vs reference MCMC) as function of N.

3. Change the order / what waits on what: within-time-series parallelism — the model is a sequential recursion over time steps; but likelihood could be decomposed: compute per-timestep log-likelihoods given state summaries... Actually the recursion is the state update. Alternative: parallel-in-time methods, or change the data unit: split long time series into independent event-based segments (storm events), calibrate on events in parallel — changes the unit of work from "full chain over full record" to "independent event posteriors" that can be merged. Assumption: calibration must use the entire continuous record; events may be nearly sufficient.

4. Change the objective: replace sampling with variational inference or normalizing flows; or replace "posterior of parameters" with "ranking of parameter sets" or "yes/no whether model can reproduce observed behavior" (limits of acceptability, GLUE). Hmm, GLUE is prior.

5. Ask whether mixing time is the blocker vs per-step cost: measure autocorrelation time / ESS per second. If ESS per second is dominated by serial correlation (multimodality, correlated params), then GPU parallelism buys nothing unless you change the proposal geometry — reparameterization, Riemannian HMC, or population MCMC with adaptive proposals. Reparameterization is cheap: whiten the posterior using a pilot run — compute after: same model runs but each sample worth 10-100x more.

Also: the likelihood itself — residual error model; changing what's measured (data): use summary statistics of streamflow (signatures) instead of full hydrograph — likelihood-free ABC; signatures reduce the data dimension and make likelihood cheap and parallelizable, but lose information — measure whether posterior on parameters using signatures matches full-data posterior.

Let me pick three strong reframings aligned with the guidance: alter what more compute buys.

Reframe 1 — objective: from full posterior samples to posterior predictive quantities / tail estimates via amortized SBI. Actually let me structure:

Reframe A (unit of work + what compute buys): Replace sequential MCMC with amortized simulation-based inference (neural posterior estimation). The serial dependence (chain step waits on previous step) is the blocker; simulation is embarrassingly parallel. Assumption: posterior must be built by a Markov chain where each step waits on the previous; must evaluate likelihood sequentially. Reframe: precompute a large parallel bank of (parameter, data) simulations on GPU, train a density estimator, evaluate posterior for any catchment instantly. Question: How many simulator runs does NPE need so the posterior-predictive distribution (or parameter posterior) is within a fixed tolerance (e.g., C2ST < 0.6, or MMD) of a long reference MCMC for a set of catchments? Measure: run N ∈ {1e3..1e6} simulations in parallel, train NPE, compute C2ST/MMD/ESS-equivalent vs reference; cheapest: one catchment, N up to 1e5, each run ~10 ms on CPU → trivial GPU cost, maybe 1 GPU-day. Cost estimate: GR4J runs ~ microseconds-milliseconds; 1e5 runs = minutes. So cheap: a laptop day.

Reframe B (what is measured / objective): Change from estimating the full parameter posterior to estimating a small set of decision-relevant predictive quantities (e.g., distribution of 100-year flood quantile, or P(flow > threshold)), possibly via sequential Monte Carlo / importance sampling targeted at the quantity, or emulating the map parameters→quantity directly with a GP and active learning. This changes more compute from "more of the same samples" to "converge the tail quantity." Question: Does active learning on the map (parameters → flood quantile estimate) reduce the number of model evaluations needed to reach ±5% error on the 1%-exceedance quantile vs a 1e5-step MCMC, by an order of magnitude? Measure: number of likelihood evaluations to convergence of the quantity. Cost: one catchment, pilot: a few CPU-days.

Reframe C (order of steps / what waits on what): parallel-in-time or event-based decomposition of the likelihood. Assumption: calibration must run the model over the full continuous record in sequence. Reframe: split record into hydrologically independent storm events with warmup; compute per-event log-likelihoods in parallel (or calibrate per-event posteriors and combine). Question: What fraction of the total wall-clock and what fraction of posterior information (Fisher info / posterior variance) comes from event segments vs inter-event periods — i.e., does an event-only likelihood recover the same posterior? Measure: run per-event calibration, compare posteriors (Wasserstein distance) with full-record posterior; measure speedup per core count. Cost: small.

Alternatively Reframe C could be reparameterization/proposal geometry: the assumption that the chain must walk in the original parameterization with isotropic proposals; measure ESS per likelihood call after whitening / using DREAM-ZS / HMC with surrogate gradients. Question: what is ESS per model evaluation before/after reparameterization — measured by a pilot run. That's the cheapest diagnostic of all: first measure where time goes: per-step cost vs autocorrelation. Actually a key first thing: "Find where this problem stops more compute from helping": MCMC mixing time is serial — a chain of length T gives ESS ~ T/τ_int; more GPUs let you run more chains but ESS grows linearly only with independent work; the blocker is autocorrelation time τ_int, set by posterior geometry (multimodality, correlations), not by hardware. So compute buys "more of the same": running 1000 chains of length T doesn't reduce τ_int; you need shorter τ_int (geometry) or a different estimator (SBI).

Also per-step cost may be trivial for lumped models — long MCMC needed not because each step is expensive but because of multimodality and parameter correlation (equifinality). So "shit ton of GPU parallelism" only helps if you parallelize the right unit: independent chains (limited by τ), or simulations for amortized inference (unbounded parallelism).

Let me also consider: measure-first diagnostic: profile ESS/minute: if per-sample cost is microseconds and τ_int is 1e4 steps, the fix is geometry, not GPUs. The question asks for reframes ending with a question someone could investigate, specific, answerable by measurement, naming what is measured; plus cheapest measurement with rough cost.

Schema fields per reframe:
- bottleneck: where compute stops helping
- assumption: the held-fixed assumption
- reframe: the change
- question: specific investigable question naming what is measured
- measure: cheapest measurement + rough cost
- compute_after: what more compute buys after the reframe
- exact: ? Possibly "exact" = what exact/quantitative result would confirm? Hmm. Fields: "exact" and "expected" — likely: exact = the exact quantity/threshold to be measured / precise prediction; expected = expected outcome. Or "exact" = what would be exactly true / precise statement. I'll interpret: exact = the precise quantitative criterion that would confirm the reframe works (exact metric/threshold); expected = what you expect to find; fails_if = condition under which the idea fails / is not worth pursuing; closest_prior = closest prior work.

Closest prior for SBI in hydrology: neural posterior estimation (Papamakarios & Murray 2016; Lueckmann et al. 2017; Cranmer et al. 2020 "The frontier of simulation-based inference"); hydrology application: e.g., "Amortized Bayesian inference of groundwater models" or SBI for hydrological models — there are works applying SBI to rainfall-runoff (e.g., "Simulation-based inference for rainfall-runoff models"?). Known prior: DREAM(ZS) (Vrugt et al. 2009), GLUE (Beven & Binley 1992), hydrologic signatures (McMillan et al.), SMC (Chopin), parallel tempering, surrogate/emulator calibration (e.g., GP emulation, polynomial chaos for hydrological models — Reichert et al.), event-based calibration. Variational inference for hydrology. Also "Bayesian inference of hydrological models with emulators" (Razavi et al. surrogate modeling review). FLOOD / quantile estimation: importance sampling for rare events. Active learning with GPs for likelihood (e.g., Bayesian optimization of likelihood — Kandasamy; "Bayesian Active Learning for Posterior Estimation" — Kandasamy et al. 2017; Järvenpää et al.).

Let me now pick the three reframes:

1. Bottleneck: MCMC's serial dependence — each likelihood evaluation waits on the previous; posterior geometry (equifinality, multimodality) sets autocorrelation time τ_int, so ESS grows only linearly with wall-clock and parallel chains don't shorten τ_int. GPU parallelism buys more of the same.
   Assumption: the posterior must be approximated by a Markov chain over the original parameter space; inference must be per-catchment, from scratch.
   Reframe: change the unit of work from chain-steps to independent model simulations: amortized neural posterior estimation. Generate (θ, x) pairs in massive GPU parallel batches, train a conditional density estimator once (possibly across many catchments), then obtain posteriors instantly.
   Question: measured: number of simulations N needed for NPE posterior to match reference MCMC within tolerance (C2ST accuracy < 0.6 or posterior-predictive NSE...). "For K catchments, at what N does the C2ST classifier accuracy between NPE posterior samples and a 10^6-step DREAM reference fall below 0.55?"
   Measure: one catchment (e.g., GR4J on a MOPEX/CAMELS basin, 10 years daily). Simulate N = 1e3..3e5 parameter draws (CPU ms each, ~10 min total or seconds on GPU), train NPE (minutes on one GPU), compute C2ST vs reference chain. Cost: ~1 GPU-day total including reference chain (reference DREAM 1e5 evals at ms each = minutes). So a day on a workstation.
   Compute_after: each extra GPU-hour raises N and directly lowers posterior error — compute converts to accuracy rather than to more correlated samples; also amortizes across catchments (train once for 500 CAMELS basins, inference free for new basins).
   Exact: the N–error curve (log-log slope of C2ST or MMD vs N) for one basin; success = error ≤ tolerance at N ≤ 1e5.
   Expected: NPE matches MCMC with ~1e4–1e5 simulations for a 5–10 parameter lumped model; GPU wall-clock minutes vs days of MCMC; biggest win when amortized over many catchments.
   Fails_if: likelihood error-model parameters (heteroscedastic noise) make the posterior too sharp/multimodal so NPE needs >1e7 sims, or the simulator is deterministic-but-chaotic making the regression ill-conditioned; also fails if the inference must condition on data far outside the training distribution (nonstationary climate).
   Closest_prior: Cranmer et al. 2020 SBI review; Lueckmann NPE; applied: SBI for hydrologic models (e.g., "Neural density estimation for conceptual hydrologic models"); also GLUE/DREAM(ZS) as incumbent (Vrugt 2009).

2. Bottleneck: objective is "the full parameter posterior," so every sample costs a full-record simulation even though decisions depend on a few predictive functionals; long chains are spent resolving parameter directions that don't move predictions.
   Assumption: the quantity to estimate is the posterior over all parameters; predictions come afterwards as a derived product.
   Reframe: change the measured quantity: directly target the posterior of predictive quantities (e.g., the 1% exceedance flow, reservoir-yield reliability) using emulation + active learning / importance reweighting; compute concentrates near the region of parameter space that controls the quantity (including tails).
   Question: measured: number of model evaluations to reach ±5% (relative) error in the posterior mean and 95% interval of the 100-year flood quantile, for targeted active-learning-GP vs full MCMC then propagate. "Does a GP-emulated, actively-targeted estimator reach the tolerance in ≤1e3 evaluations where MCMC needs 1e5?"
   Measure: pick one basin and one quantity; run DREAM reference (1e5 evals) to get ground truth quantile distribution; then run GP active learning (expected improvement on the functional) with budget 500–2000 evals; compare bias/RMSE of the quantile estimate vs evaluation count. Cost: a few CPU-days (lumped model ms per run) — a weekend on a laptop or 1 node-day.
   Compute_after: extra compute shrinks error on the decision quantity directly and can be aimed at the tail (rare events) where MCMC is weakest — each new evaluation is placed where it changes the answer, not drawn from the same chain.
   Exact: RMSE of the 100-year quantile estimate vs number of evaluations, threshold ±5% with 90% confidence over repeated runs.
   Expected: 10–100x fewer evaluations for smooth low-dimensional functionals; less gain if the quantile is controlled by a rough, wide region.
   Fails_if: the mapping θ→quantile is discontinuous/highly multimodal (threshold effects, snow processes), so GP emulation needs as many points as MCMC; or if the decision truly needs the full joint posterior (multi-objective).
   Closest_prior: Bayesian active learning for posterior estimation (Kandasamy et al. 2017), GP emulation of hydrological models (Reichert et al. 2011; Razavi et al. 2012 review), importance sampling / subset simulation for rare-event estimation (Au & Beck 2001).

3. Bottleneck: order of steps: the model's time recursion forces a full continuous simulation over decades per likelihood call, and the chain is long because the likelihood treats every timestep as equally informative; wall-clock and chain length both scale with record length.
   Assumption: calibration must use the entire continuous hydrograph in one sequential run; all timesteps carry comparable information about parameters.
   Reframe: reorder/cut the work: decompose the record into near-independent storm events (with short warm-up), calibrate event posteriors in parallel and combine (consensus Bayes), or use event-only likelihood; the unit of work becomes an event, which is short and independent → embarrassingly parallel and much shorter serial chains. Alternative phrasing: per-event likelihoods computed in parallel across time — "parallel over data" rather than over chains.
   Question: measured: fraction of Fisher information (or posterior variance reduction) about each parameter contributed by event segments vs inter-event baseflow periods, and the Wasserstein distance between the event-only posterior and the full-record posterior. "Do event segments (say, top 5% of timesteps by flow) carry ≥90% of the information while cutting serial simulation length by ≥10x?"
   Measure: one basin: compute per-timestep parameter sensitivity (Jacobian of simulated flow) or run calibration on event-only data vs full record; compare posteriors (W2 distance, coverage) and wall-clock per ESS. Cost: hours-days on one core; ~1 CPU-day.
   Compute_after: after reframe, more compute = more events/catchments in parallel and shorter serial recursions per call, so GPUs reduce wall-clock directly rather than adding correlated samples.
   Exact: information share of event timesteps per parameter (sensitivity-based) and W2(event posterior, full posterior) normalized by posterior std; success if ≥90% info from ≤10% of timesteps and W2 ≤ 0.1σ.
   Expected: most parameters (quickflow, routing) identified almost entirely from events; baseflow parameters need recession segments — so a two-block decomposition rather than full record; expect 5–20x serial-length cut.
   Fails_if: the model's state memory (e.g., groundwater store) couples events across seasons so event posteriors can't be merged without bias; then information is spread across the full record and decomposition biases posterior.
   Closest_prior: hydrological signatures / event-based calibration (McMillan et al. on signatures; "Diagnosis of model structure" via events), consensus/embarrassingly parallel MCMC (Scott et al. 2016 consensus Monte Carlo; Neiswanger et al. 2014), parallel-in-time ODE/SDE methods.

Maybe I should also mention the pure diagnostic: measure ESS/hour decomposition (per-eval cost vs τ_int) — but reframes are asked. I'll embed in bottleneck text.

Also compute_after field: "what more compute buys after the reframe."

"exact": I'll interpret as the exact quantitative success criterion — the precise measurable threshold that would confirm.

Ensure JSON is valid, one object with "reframes" array of 3 objects. No markdown, only JSON.

Costs: rough: "1 GPU-day", "a laptop-weekend (~2 CPU-days)", etc. Lumped models like GR4J run ~1e-4–1e-3 s per year of daily data; 40-year record → ~5–50 ms per eval; 1e5 evals ≈ 1–2 hours serial. Distributed models are slower (seconds-minutes). I'll keep estimates plausible.

Write concise but complete strings.

Let me draft final JSON.

Reframe 1 strings:

bottleneck: "MCMC is serial: each likelihood evaluation waits on the previous one, and effective sample size grows as T/τ_int where the autocorrelation time τ_int is set by posterior geometry (parameter correlation, equifinality, multimodality), not by hardware. More GPUs only run more of the same correlated chains; τ_int is unchanged. For lumped models each step costs milliseconds, so compute is not the blocker — mixing is."

assumption: "The posterior must be built by a Markov chain run from scratch for each catchment, and the only way to spend compute is more chain steps or more chains."

reframe: "Change the unit of work from chain steps to independent simulator runs: amortized simulation-based inference. Draw parameters from a proposal, run the rainfall-runoff model in massively parallel GPU batches, and train a neural posterior estimator once (possibly across hundreds of catchments). Inference for any basin then costs one forward pass, and every extra GPU-hour lowers posterior error instead of adding correlated samples."

question: "For a benchmark basin set (e.g., 10 CAMELS catchments with GR4J), how many simulations N does neural posterior estimation need before the C2ST classifier accuracy between NPE samples and a 1e6-step DREAM reference posterior falls below 0.55 (chance-level)?"

measure: "Run the reference DREAM chain once (1e5–1e6 evals at ~5–50 ms each: a few CPU-hours), then N = 1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6 simulations in parallel batches (minutes on one GPU) and train NPE (~1 GPU-hour). Measure C2ST and MMD vs the reference as a function of N. Rough cost: 1 GPU-day plus one CPU-day."

compute_after: "Each additional GPU-hour increases N and directly reduces posterior approximation error, with near-linear parallel scaling; amortized across catchments, the marginal cost of calibrating a new basin drops to ~zero."

exact: "The error-vs-N curve: C2ST(N) and MMD(N) against the reference; success = C2ST < 0.55 (and posterior-predictive NSE within 0.01 of MCMC) at N ≤ 1e5 for at least 8 of 10 basins."

expected: "For a 6–10 parameter lumped model with a smooth likelihood, NPE reaches tolerance at N ≈ 1e4–1e5 — minutes of GPU time versus days of serial MCMC, with the gain compounding when one network serves many basins."

fails_if: "Including observation-noise/error-model parameters makes the posterior sharply multimodal so C2ST stays above 0.55 even at N ≥ 1e6 (density estimator can't resolve the modes), or basins outside the training distribution need per-basin retraining that eats the amortization gain."

closest_prior: "Cranmer, Brehmer & Louppe 2020 (SBI review) and Lueckmann et al. 2017 (NPE); DREAM(ZS) as incumbent (Vrugt et al. 2009); early SBI applications to conceptual hydrologic models (e.g., neural density estimation for HBV-type models, 2022–2024)."

Reframe 2:

bottleneck: "The objective is the full joint parameter posterior, but every chain step pays for a full-record simulation and spends samples resolving parameter directions (equifinality ridges) that barely move any decision-relevant prediction. Compute buys more samples of quantities nobody uses, and tail predictions (the part that matters for flood design) converge slowest of all."

assumption: "One must first estimate the whole parameter posterior and only then propagate it to predictions; the quantity to estimate is fixed as the posterior itself."

reframe: "Change what is measured: estimate the decision quantity directly — e.g., the posterior distribution of the 1%-exceedance (100-year) flood quantile — by emulating the map from parameters (and error model) to that quantity with a Gaussian process and choosing evaluation points actively (Bayesian active learning for posterior estimation), with importance sampling targeted at the tail. Compute is spent only where it changes the quantity."

question: "Does GP emulation with active point selection estimate the posterior mean and 95% interval of the 100-year flood quantile to within ±5% (relative) using ≤1e3 model evaluations, where brute MCMC propagation needs ≥1e5, for a set of 10 basins?"

measure: "On one basin, get ground truth from a long DREAM run propagated to the quantile (a few CPU-hours). Then run the active-learning GP with budgets 250–2000 evaluations, repeat 10 times for variance, and record relative RMSE vs evaluation count. Rough cost: one laptop-weekend (~2 CPU-days)."

compute_after: "Extra evaluations are placed where the functional is most uncertain or most tail-heavy, so added compute shrinks error on the quantity itself — including the rare tail where plain MCMC is weakest — rather than lengthening a chain."

exact: "RMSE(relative error of quantile posterior mean and interval) vs number of evaluations; success = ≤5% relative error with ≥90% confidence at ≤1e3 evaluations, i.e., ≥100x fewer evaluations than the MCMC reference."

expected: "For smooth low-dimensional functionals of a lumped model, expect 10–100x reduction in evaluations; gain shrinks if the quantile is controlled by a wide, flat region of parameter space (strong equifinality in the prediction itself)."

fails_if: "The parameter-to-quantile map is discontinuous or oscillatory (threshold/snow/switching processes) so GP emulation needs ~as many points as MCMC, or stakeholders actually need the full joint posterior for multiple, changing objectives."

closest_prior: "Kandasamy et al. 2017 (Bayesian active learning for posterior estimation); GP/polynomial-chaos emulation of hydrological models (Reichert et al. 2011; Razavi et al. 2012 review); subset simulation for rare events (Au & Beck 2001)."

Reframe 3:

bottleneck: "Both chain length and per-step cost scale with the full continuous record: the model's state recursion forces a decades-long sequential simulation for every likelihood evaluation, and the likelihood weights every timestep equally even though only a few percent of timesteps (storm events, recessions) constrain parameters. The serial dependency over time is the part that waits and need not."

assumption: "Calibration must run the model continuously over the whole record and all timesteps are equally informative; time cannot be cut without biasing inference."

reframe: "Cut and reorder the unit of work: decompose the record into near-independent hydrologic events (with short warm-up) plus recession blocks, calibrate each block in parallel, and combine the block posteriors (consensus Bayes) — or use an event-only likelihood. The serial unit shrinks from decades to days, and blocks are embarrassingly parallel."

question: "Measured per parameter: what fraction of the posterior information (1/posterior-variance, or integrated parameter sensitivity) comes from event and recession segments covering ≤10% of timesteps, and what is the Wasserstein-2 distance between the event-block-combined posterior and the full-record posterior, in units of posterior standard deviation?"

measure: "On one basin: compute per-timestep Jacobians of simulated flow w.r.t. parameters (one simulation + adjoint or finite differences — minutes), aggregate information by segment type; then calibrate event-only and full-record posteriors (each a few CPU-hours) and compare W2 distance, coverage and wall-clock per effective sample. Rough cost: 1–2 CPU-days."

compute_after: "After the cut, more compute parallelizes across events, recessions and basins simultaneously, and each likelihood call is a short recursion — so GPUs reduce wall-clock directly instead of producing more correlated draws of a slow serial chain."

exact: "Success = segments covering ≤10% of timesteps carry ≥90% of per-parameter information AND combined event posterior within W2 ≤ 0.1σ of the full-record posterior, with ≥10x reduction in serial simulation length per likelihood call."

expected: "Quickflow, routing and event-scale parameters are identified almost entirely from events; baseflow and water-balance parameters from recession/low-flow blocks — so a two-block decomposition keeps nearly all information while cutting serial length 5–20x."

fails_if: "A slow store (groundwater/snow) with memory longer than any block couples events across seasons, so block posteriors cannot be merged without bias and the full-record recursion is genuinely necessary."

closest_prior: "Consensus/embarrassingly parallel MCMC (Scott et al. 2016; Neiswanger et al. 2014); hydrologic-signature and event-based calibration literature (McMillan et al. 2011+; 'limits of acceptability' work); parallel-in-time integration methods as the general family."

Check schema: required fields all present. Values strings. Return only JSON.

Format considerations: The instruction says return only one JSON value with no other text. So output raw JSON. I can pretty-print it — that's still one JSON value. Keep strings free of line breaks (fine in JSON if escaped; better keep single-line strings).
